description: About Project Fihrist Project Fihrist is an interdisciplinary Universal Event team led by an undergraduate student in Physics and Informatics at Dushanbe Innovation Institute. Named after the classical concept of a comprehensive index (Fihrist)—and inspired by the intersection of historical astronomical scholarship, early spaceflight milestones, and modern computational science—our mission is to turn raw NASA open data into clear, interactive, and scientifically grounded tools.
summary: Fihrist reads 24 years of NASA data for any field and compares three crop rotations on water, soil nitrogen, food and risk. Every number traces to a dataset or a cited source.
details:
Farmers in Tajikistan and northern Afghanistan face 40 °C summers, shared irrigation water and soils drained by continuous wheat or cotton. Climate, water, soil and nutrition are usually analysed in separate tools. Fihrist ("index" in Persian and Arabic) connects them in one auditable index.

A farmer or extension agent outlines a field on a 3D globe, or picks one of four presets. Fihrist fetches daily NASA POWER weather for 2001–2024 and runs transparent equations:

  • FAO-56 Penman–Monteith evapotranspiration
  • a daily FAO-56 soil-water balance
  • FAO-33 yield response
  • a nitrogen balance
  • USDA nutrition values

It compares the farmer's current rotation, which they can edit, with a water-saving and a regenerative rotation. Each rotation card gives: why it is suggested, the NASA evidence, expected benefits, data gaps, and local risks. Monte Carlo runs over 2,400 futures give P10/P50/P90 bands. Climate sliders test +3.5 °C and −40 % rain. Farmers can split their field into plots in 3D and assign a rotation to each one.

For any field worldwide, Fihrist computes 24 years of satellite layers on demand in about 20 seconds: MODIS NDVI over cropland, soil wetness and slope. It runs as an Azure Function next to the Microsoft Planetary Computer data.

Fihrist's compound-stress index combines heat, dryness, root-zone soil wetness and crop greenness. It flags months where crops were much less green than usual while weather and soil water were normal. All three Central Asian sites show this in March–April 2012. A winter-cold signal links it to an abnormally cold February/March 2012. We present this as a hypothesis to confirm with farmers.

Validation: in Kansas, simulated rainfed wheat follows USDA NASS yields with r = 0.77 (8 of 9 years in the same direction). The mean level is 45 % too low; we report that gap rather than tune it away.

The tool works in English, Russian and Tajik, runs on phones, and supports rather than replaces farmer and agronomist judgment.

NASA data used:

  • NASA POWER (daily and monthly; T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN, PRECTOTCORR, ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, WS2M, RH2M, GWETROOT)
  • MODIS Terra MOD13Q1 NDVI
  • NASADEM elevation

Other data and tools:

  • ESA WorldCover 2021
  • Microsoft Planetary Computer and Microsoft Azure
  • FAO-56 and FAO-33
  • USDA FoodData Central and USDA NASS
  • World Bank commodity prices
  • Meteomatics
  • OpenStreetMap / Photon, Esri World Imagery
  • Cloudflare Pages
  • React, MapLibre GL, Leaflet, Recharts

Use of AI:
The code, tests and documentation were developed with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code by Anthropic) under the team's direction and review. All scientific equations and constants come from cited sources (SOURCES.md). The app makes no AI-generated claims.

Future work:

  • 10-day heat, frost and rain warnings (Meteomatics, already running on our Azure backend)
  • crop-pattern detection from the NDVI curve
  • AI explanations in Tajik, Russian and Dari that may only use numbers the app computed
  • a Telegram bot and SMS alerts for farmers without internet
  • accounts for farmers, scientists and organisations
  • an open API for partners
  • a comparison of Earth farms with NASA's closed-chamber crop experiments on the same self-sufficiency metrics
